stories.headline: Native Hawaiian snails face extinction as funding is cut
stories.summary: More than half of Hawaii's 760 native snail species are extinct and Trump cut over $600,000 from a Bishop Museum project, while a segment describes kahuli conservation efforts including snail fences on Lānaʻi.
stories.text: Hawaiʻi stands out as one of the most biologically diverse places on earth. While we don't often think of snails as being particularly remarkable, Hawaiʻi's kahuli tree snails, brightly colored with stripes and swirls, stand out as one of the jewels of our nation. Native forests. The very fact that there are terrestrial snails in Hawaiʻi in the first place is extraordinary. Hawaiʻi is thousands of miles from any large landmass, and somehow the snails made it here over or across a saltwater ocean that is deadly to them. But regardless of how they got here, those small numbers of snails that made it radiated and evolved into probably over a thousand species, spreading into available ecological niches. Kahuli were so numerous in places that Paniolo told stories of being able to collect them by the saddlebag as they rode through the bushes. Hawaiians included kahuli in a number of oli. They made leis from their shells, and it was thought that they sang songs in the forest that you could hear at night. Sadly, their story, like so many other endemic Hawaiian species, is a sad one. Decades of overgrazing, forestry, unsustainable agricultural practices, and the introduction of numerous invasive species has caused major habitat loss. And by one estimate, over 75% of Hawaiʻi's kahuli have gone extinct in the last 100 years. Protecting the remaining populations of kahuli is crucial to their long-term survival. For instance, the island of Lānaʻi has two endemic kahuli that are found nowhere else on Earth. Unfortunately, the known number of individuals for each of these species is less than 100, and they are both at risk of extinction without protection. One tool used on lanaʻi in the last few years are pākahuli, or snail fences. These are specialized fences that enclose small areas of native forest and exclude rats, non-native snails, and chameleons with a variety of barriers. The relative protection inside the fences should allow lanaʻi's kahuli to survive in healthy numbers while we work to restore habitat and eliminate predators. Hopefully with these efforts, the song of the kahuli won't fade from the island of lanaʻi.

stories.headline: Coastal flooding alert and Huliau sea level rise strategies
stories.summary: The National Weather Service issued a statewide coastal flooding alert through Thursday afternoon, followed by a Huliau Leadership Council segment on sea level rise adaptation strategies.
stories.text: Here in Hawaiʻi, the local government is planning a projected one meter in sea level rise by the year 2100. Many of the coastlines in Hawaiʻi are being threatened by sea level rise in three main ways. First, 80% of all Maui beaches are facing coastal erosion, which The storm threatens beaches, buildings, and infrastructure. Erosion can also affect near-shore water quality, causing silt and other particles to damage the reefs. A second impact is high wave damage and flooding during storm and high wave events. The seasonal swells will affect all of the East Coast and will cause more damage as sea levels continue to rise. Finally, both coastal and inland areas will become vulnerable to flooding, mostly during high tides, Resulting in rising groundwater tables and drain system failures. This can also cause saltwater intrusion, threatening our wildlife habitats, agriculture, and our supply of fresh drinking water. Because areas can be impacted by one or all of these impacts, different adaptation strategies are used in different areas to address these impacts. One adaptation strategy, cloud protection, physically blocks higher sea levels and keeps the shoreline from moving inland. One example is seawalls, which is a form of coastal defense, which help protect against waves and high tides. Another example of protection, which you see here in front of Sands of Kahana, are sandbags that are used to construct a temporary protective wall, or a barrier to hold back flood waters. A second adaptation strategy, which is accommodation, where development is modified in place to make it more resilient to sea level rise, such as raising houses on stilts as a protection against flooding. The ecosystem-based adaptation uses the conservation and restoration of natural systems to lessen the impact of sea level rise on shorelines. Here in Maui, a lot of community groups and sea level rise experts are taking the ecosystem-based adaptation approach and protecting our beaches. Like here in Kamaole 1, where local volunteers have been working to promote dune health by planting native species. In the case of dunes, they are used to prevent aegis from eroding away because they act like a sand-savage account during times where a lot of sand is being removed due to high-wave action. But in some cases, unfortunately, the shoreline is too forgotten to be protected or restored, and in those instances, must retreat or move farther inland. While there aren't any properties actively planning for retreat here in Maui, this is a potential reality facing a lot of developments placed close to Maui shorelines. Maui County is proposing new shoreline setback rules that would prevent future developments from being placed too close to shorelines, ensure safer location of structures in the long run, and to restore natural buffers. When choosing how to adapt to sea level rise, it is important to look at the disadvantages and advantages of these four strategies. For example, protections such as seawalls do help but only in the short term. While they protect oceanfront buildings, they can eventually create erosion outside of the wall. On the other hand, retreat or permanently moving structures is a long-term solution but very expensive. While it keeps a community safe, it can force people out of their homes and businesses. Here at Baldwin Beach, the moving of the bathrooms and showers inland is a small example of retreat. However, Baldwin Beach is a place where the community can get involved in adaptation planning and where ecosystem restoration may help to preserve and restore natural buffers. The longest term solutions involve building resilience or building back better. Initially creating infrastructure with climate change in mind can allow for increased savings and safety. It's important to share this knowledge with your ʻohana and community. Working together as a community is a vital element in building resilience.

stories.headline: Shark webinar announced; study tracks Maui tiger sharks
stories.summary: The Maui Nui Marine Resource Council invites the public to a free Why Sharks Matter webinar, followed by a package on UH research tracking tiger sharks around Maui and Oʻahu.
stories.text: Important research out of the University of Hawaiʻi is providing state leaders with critical information to better develop outreach and awareness efforts to minimize possibly dangerous encounters with tiger sharks. After a spike in shark bites off of Maui in 2012 and 2013, the State Department of Land and Natural Resources turned to the experts at the UH Mānoa Hawaiʻi Institute of Marine Biology. In 2016, UH shark researchers Carl Meyer, Kim Holland, and a team of students completed an important study revealing movement patterns of tiger sharks around Maui and Oʻahu. We tagged 41 sharks around Maui and Oʻahu and then we tracked their movements for two years. And what we found was that the Maui sharks spent most of their time over insular shelf habitat, which is the area between the beach and the shelf break that occurs at a depth of around 600 feet. And this shelf habitat contains a wide variety of the types of prey that tiger sharks like to eat. And Maui nui has more of this habitat than all of the other main Hawaiian islands combined. This attracts tiger sharks from the rest of Hawaiʻi, and the sharks that regularly reside in the large shelf habitat off of Maui are less likely to travel away from the area. The study also found that the Maui tiger sharks occasionally frequent popular beaches. Now although tiger sharks are routinely present in waters where we swim, surf and dive, the risk of being bitten is actually still very low, and this suggests that tiger sharks are generally avoiding interactions with people. The study also discredits the practice of shark culling, where the creatures are hunted and killed to reduce the risks of bites. Well, we now know when we look back at those historic efforts that they had absolutely no effect on either eliminating or reducing the number of bites that occurred. There is a wealth of shark data available to the public through an online mapping platform from the Pacific Islands Ocean Observing System at the UH Mānoa School of Ocean and Earth Science and Technology. Where anybody can go online and can see these sharks moving around, and that helps the public We need to understand that these animals are naturally present in the waters where they swim and surf. UH's Pacific Islands Ocean Observing System and the Hawaii Institute of Marine Biology will continue to bring animal tracking to the next level through advanced satellite tagging. Sharks and other large pelagic fish can serve as an excellent resource to collect ocean observation data and increase our understanding of ocean dynamics.

stories.summary: The Hapapa Watershed Deer Damage Mitigation Project announced completion of a year and a half pilot to revegetate and stabilize 11 acres devastated by feral Axis deer, followed by a segment on deer population growth.
stories.text: The carrying capacity of the islands is critical especially in island ecosystems. When the carrying capacity is exceeded, environmental degradation begins such as erosion and changes in the water cycle and plant community. Over the last several years, there has been evidence that the carrying capacity of rangelands in Maui County is being exceeded, in particular with regard to access to deer which roam freely on all three islands in the county. It is important that everyone on Maui, Molokaʻi, and Lānaʻi understands this situation. These islands are home to us all and the condition of the land affects not only us but future generations. Lands that are overgrazed can push damage to a tipping point of irreversible ecological damage. There is a limit to how many animals our lands can carry and still be healthy. To help illustrate what is happening, let us walk through a scenario based on some assumptions about the deer herd on Maui. In this example, one of these equals a thousand deer. In early 2022, a survey was done that found about 46,000 deer on part of Maui. Let's assume the deer population on Maui is 50,000 deer. Based on herd observations, it is estimated the herd is mostly female. So let's assume that 80% or 40,000 deer are female. Axis deer are known to be prolific producers. We will assume 90% of all the female deer give birth to one fawn each year, So that the herd will grow by 36,000 deer each year. According to reports, roughly 16,000 deer were hunted or harvested in 2022. Since this harvest rate is less than the estimated reproductive rate, we can logically conclude the herd will continue to grow. After one year, the herd is now up to 70,000, with more females reproducing and the herd growing again. If the numbers were too high at 50,000, causing overgrazing that was hurting the environment, The damage will get even worse every year unless we turn this around and start moving towards balancing the system. We can't make more land. We can't make it rain. The number of animals needs to be managed. Continued overgrazing by excessive wildlife populations will cause further degradation of land and near shore waters in Maui County. stories.text: This was once a thriving plantation, a place of history. For nearly a hundred years, the economy was all about huge farms. Sugar and pineapple were everything. The artifacts, these forgotten pieces of machinery, tell stories of generations who worked here, the diverse cultures creating the Maui community. People came from all over. They were hoping for a better life. They worked so hard, from morning till night, for very little pay. They poured their lives into this land, but sadly, they rarely saw the vast wealth they helped create. And with the hard work, there was always the stunning natural beauty, the lush gardens filled with color and life. Here, the air is alive. stories.headline: Work begins clearing 42 acres of wildfire fuel in Ukumehame
stories.summary: Crews began removing brush, debris and 160 abandoned vehicles from a high-risk site in Ukumehame, and a county segment describes the restoration plans.
stories.text: InʻUkumehame there is this area that's been used as a dump site. We pulled about 150 abandoned vehicles out of there last year and saw all the trash. We also learned that this area has wetland features, and so not only did we want to get the trash out, but we realized this was an ecologically significant and sensitive area. So we wanted to give it extra attention to hopefully restore some of those wetland features in the coming years. We're calling it the Hoʻola ʻĀina Restoration Project. So at Abandoned Vehicles and Metals, we know how to clean up cars and trash, but we really needed help and advice from many other community partners. Malama Maui Nui is helping us with the trash cleanup. We also have talked to community partners right in Ukumehame and Oluwalu to get their advice about how to properly enhance this area. We walked the property with the principal archaeologists for the county as well as some cultural practitioners, and they indicated that this is also a highly culturally historical place. We also know that this was an area that was used for sugar cane, And so we wanted to get a water pit that we found in that area tested to see what kind of contaminants were in that pit. Eventually we are hoping to have the area cleaned up and then retest to see if those levels of contaminants have gone down. A lot of the trash is mixed and buried tightly with the trees. Most of the trees are invasive, so we'll be removing the invasive trees by hand and leaving all of the native and canoe trees in place. We're going to be doing this project in phases, and that's to allow the water table to stabilize once we remove the first round of invasive trees. We're also hoping that as we clean up the trash and remove some of the invasive species, over time we can introduce seeds and seedlings that will begin to enhance the moisture in the area, not just only the moisture in the soil, but the moisture in the air. All of that helps to invite other natives Our hopes for this project are to turn this into an ecologically and culturally productive site that everybody can use once again.
